● Yes, it's clear. I've read all four files, and here is what I'll do:

  - Build: a Python app that answers questions about the three papers with
    citations, verifies the whole answer, and refuses when the papers don't say.
    It runs on Groq's gpt-oss-120b, with gpt-oss-20b as the fallback. A Go
    stand-in model service and a Go load generator handle the scenarios Groq's
    free tier can't take.
  - Order: I'll follow the build order in DESIGN.md §20.1. Phase 1 (fetch the
    papers at their exact versions, then hybrid retrieval) comes first, and
    phase 2 (one request working end to end, with a caught unsupported claim and
    a correct refusal) comes before any queue, rate governor or stand-in work.
  - Rules from CLAUDE.md:
    - I won't make a real Groq call until I've told you how many calls and
      tokens it will use and you've said yes.
    - The API key stays only in .env.
    - Table numbers come only from results.csv.
    - I won't touch anything already in results/raw/.
    - After every unit I'll write its tests, run the full suite, and report the
      results to you.

  Things to sort out before I start:

  1. File locations don't match. CLAUDE.md says the design lives at
     docs/DESIGN.md, but it's in the project root. I'll move it to docs/ so the
     files match what the design itself says, unless you'd rather keep it at the
     root.
  2. The two design docs have different authors. The architecture doc is signed
     "@Priyanshu Yadav" and DESIGN.md is signed "Akash Bisht". The brief looks
     for work that is distinctly yours, so check that byline before you submit.
  3. A small mismatch inside the architecture doc. It says 11 nodes but its
     table lists 10, leaving out return_answer. DESIGN.md lists all 11, and I'll
     follow DESIGN.md.
  4. Python isn't found under python. On this machine only py (Python 3.12.3)
     works, so I'll create the venv with py -m venv .venv. Go 1.25 and git are
     installed. The folder isn't a git repo yet; I'll run git init unless you
     say otherwise.
  5. The design is large for 6–8 hours of work. It includes LangGraph, FAISS, a
     cross-encoder, a governor with token buckets, single-flight, two Go
     programs and four retrieval settings. The build order already pushes cache,
     single-flight and the optional experiments to the end, so I'll build
     exactly what each phase needs and stop there.

  Shall I start phase 1 (setup, then fetching the papers)? Downloading the
  papers from arXiv doesn't use any Groq quota.

  I haven't verified anything against Groq or arXiv yet. The main risk is the
  real-call budget: at about 57 answers a day, it needs roughly 2.5 of your 4
  days.

● The second phase 1 unit, latex_parse, is done: it turns the three papers'
  LaTeX into sections, paragraphs and tables. The full test suite passes (33
  tests). Phase 1 isn't finished yet; three units remain before phase 2.

  What it produces (in data/processed/):

  ┌───────┬──────────┬────────────┬────────┬─────────┐
  │ Paper │ Sections │ Paragraphs │ Tables │ Figures │
  ├───────┼──────────┼────────────┼────────┼─────────┤
  │ AIAYN │ 24       │ 68         │ 4      │ 5       │
  ├───────┼──────────┼────────────┼────────┼─────────┤
  │ MOSHI │ 45       │ 141        │ 19     │ 11      │
  ├───────┼──────────┼────────────┼────────┼─────────┤
  │ HNET  │ 36       │ 166        │ 8      │ 16      │
  └───────┴──────────┴────────────┴────────┴─────────┘

  - Checked against the PDFs: the table and figure counts match exactly. Every
    numbered section heading appears in its PDF, including the appendix letters.
  - Tables: each row becomes a line of text such as Transformer: BLEU / EN-DE = 
    28.4; ..., with headers and units repeated on every row.
  - References: links to sections, tables and equations resolve to real numbers
    ("see Table 3", "equation (2)"). None are left as ??, and no raw LaTeX is
    left in the paragraph text.

  Quirks in the papers I had to handle:
  - MOSHI puts two \sections inside table environments.
  - HNET puts two tables inside figures.
  - A MOSHI macro printed symbols twice ("QQ").
  - Layout commands leaked into the text, such as \looseness=-1 and the table
    colours.

  Where I deviated from DESIGN.md (recorded in §20.3):
  - \paragraph{} headings and unnumbered subsections stay inside their parent
    section instead of getting their own ID, because the PDF doesn't number them
    either.
  - All text is normalised to plain characters, so math-font letters like
    "𝖢𝗁𝗎𝗇𝗄" become "Chunk" and keyword search can match them.

  Tests:
  - Unit tests (20): brace matching, comments, \input handling, macros, text
    conversion, table parsing, section numbering, appendix lettering, and
    reference resolution.
  - Integration tests (3): a fake arXiv download goes through fetch and parse
    into JSONL, with the bibliography kept out. One test runs on the real
    downloaded papers and fails if a parser change breaks the counts that match
    the PDFs.

  Next unit: pdf_validate (DESIGN §6.3), which records a page number for each
  paragraph. After that come chunker and index_build; phase 1 is done when the
  gold passages are retrieved for the dev questions. Shall I continue?

  What I didn't check: a few inline maths fragments read oddly (for example x 
  ∈R^L), and I haven't hand-checked every table row against the PDF. I only
  spot-checked three tables. Nothing has been committed yet.

    that fails, it tries any 8-word run from the paragraph's first 40 words. The
    page goes into paragraphs.jsonl, and the coverage report goes into
    data/processed/pdf_validation.json.

    is maths-heavy. Their page is left empty. DESIGN says the page is optional
    in citations, so this doesn't block anything.

  Phase 1 so far

  Phase 1 turns the three papers into searchable pieces that answers can cite.

  1. fetch_papers (done). Downloads the three papers at their exact versions
  (v7, v1, v2) as both LaTeX source and PDF. It records a checksum for every
  file, and it refuses any paper ID without a version suffix.

  2. latex_parse (done). Reads the LaTeX and splits it into sections,
  paragraphs, tables and figure captions.
  - Numbering: sections are numbered exactly as the PDF shows them (3.2.1,
    appendix A, B, …).
  - Tables: each row becomes one line of text, such as Transformer: BLEU / EN-DE
    = 28.4, so numbers can be found and cited.
  - References: "see Table 3" and "equation (2)" resolve to the real numbers.
  - Bibliography: stored separately, so search never sees reference-list text.
  - Checked against the PDFs: 4 / 19 / 8 tables and 5 / 11 / 16 figures,
    matching exactly.

  3. pdf_validate (done). Finds each paragraph in the PDF and records its page
  number.
  - Coverage: 100% of paragraphs found in AIAYN, 100% in MOSHI and 98.8% in
    HNET.
  - Headings: every section heading was found in its PDF.
  - Bug caught: equations had been split off from their sentences. That's fixed
    in latex_parse.

  Tests: 45 tests, all passing. One of them runs on the real papers, so a later
  parser change can't quietly break the counts.

  Remaining in phase 1

  4. chunker (next). Cuts the paragraphs into pieces of about 256 and 512
  tokens. A piece never crosses a section boundary. Table rows and figure
  captions become their own pieces, and every piece gets a stable ID such as
  MOSHI:4.2:c017, which is what answers will cite.

  5. index_build, then retrieval. Builds two search indexes for each piece size:
  - Keyword search (BM25): good for exact terms like "Mimi" or "dechunking".
  - Meaning-based search (BGE-small embeddings in FAISS): finds passages that
    are worded differently from the question.

  On top of the indexes come the search code (both results merged with RRF), the
  optional reranker, and context trimming.

  Phase 1 is done when the right passages come back for the dev questions. That
  needs the eval question set (eval/questions.jsonl, 30 questions with gold
  answers and citations), which doesn't exist yet. The brief wants these
  questions written by you, since they count as "distinctly yours". I can draft
  them for you to check, or you can write them.

  After phase 1

  - Phase 2: one question goes all the way through: search, then an answer with
    citations, then a check that every claim matches its cited passage, then a
    refusal when the papers don't say. This uses a fake model, so it costs no
    Groq calls.
  - Phase 4: the first real Groq calls. I'll ask you before each run and tell
    you how many calls and tokens it will use.

  Nothing has been committed yet; tell me when you want a commit. The biggest
  schedule risk is still Groq's daily token limit (about 57 answers a day), so
  phase 4 should start within the next day or so.

● The fourth phase 1 unit, chunker, is done: it cuts the papers into the pieces
  search will return and answers will cite. It needed three small supporting
  units, so I built and tested those too. The full suite passes (70 tests). One
  unit remains in phase 1: index_build and retrieval.

  What I built:

  Unit: relay/retrieval/chunker.py
  What it does: Cuts the papers into pieces of at most 256 or 512 tokens
  ────────────────────────────────────────
  Unit: relay/verify/sentences.py
  What it does: Sentence splitter that the verifier will reuse later (§14.1). It

    doesn't split on "e.g.", "et al.", "Fig. 2", "0.1" or "§3", and keeps a
    citation with the sentence it follows
  ────────────────────────────────────────
  Unit: relay/llm/tokenizer.py
  What it does: Counts tokens with o200k_harmony, gpt-oss's own tokenizer, so
    token budgets will match Groq's counts
  ────────────────────────────────────────
  Unit: config/app.yaml, config/retrieval_settings.yaml, relay/config.py
  What it does: Config files copied from DESIGN §5.2 and §5.4, plus a loader
  that
    validates the retrieval settings

  How chunking works:
  - Text: whole paragraphs are packed into a piece while they fit. A paragraph
    too long for one piece is split at sentence ends, never mid-sentence. A
    piece never crosses a section boundary.
  - Tables: each table piece repeats the caption and a Columns: … line above its
    rows, so every row keeps its meaning when retrieved alone.
  - IDs: answers will cite pieces by stable IDs such as AIAYN:3.2.1:c011 for
    text and AIAYN:T2:r01 for table rows. Rebuilding from the same input gives
    the same IDs.
  - Page numbers: each text piece carries the page from pdf_validate.

  Result:

  ┌──────────┬───────────┬──────┬──────────┬───────────┬───────────────────┐
  │  Piece   │  Total    │ Text │ Captions │  Table    │  Largest piece    │
  │   size   │  pieces   │      │          │  pieces   │     (tokens)      │
  ├──────────┼───────────┼──────┼──────────┼───────────┼───────────────────┤
  │ 256      │ 455       │ 268  │ 51       │ 136       │ 256               │
  ├──────────┼───────────┼──────┼──────────┼───────────┼───────────────────┤
  │ 512      │ 256       │ 152  │ 37       │ 67        │ 510               │
  └──────────┴───────────┴──────┴──────────┴───────────┴───────────────────┘

  One decision, recorded in DESIGN §20.3: some table captions are long, and at
  256 tokens repeating them left room for only about 1.7 rows per piece, with 55
  pieces over the limit. Now, when a caption takes more than a quarter of a
  piece, the row pieces repeat only its first sentence and the full caption is
  stored once as its own piece. Table pieces now hold about 2.5 rows each, and
  nothing is over the limit.

  Tests: 70 passed, 0 failed.
  - Unit tests (25 new):
    - Sentence splitting: abbreviations, decimals, line breaks, citations.
    - Tokenizer: the right encoding, and long-text splitting that loses nothing.
    - Config: the files load, and invalid settings are rejected.
    - Chunker: packing, sentence and token fallbacks, table and caption pieces,
      IDs, pages, sections never mixing, stable rebuilds, one output file per
      size.
  - Integration tests: fetch, parse, validate and chunk now run together on the
    fake paper. On the real papers, at both sizes: every ID is unique, no piece
    is over its limit, and the text pieces contain exactly as many words as the
    parsed paragraphs, so no text is lost or duplicated.
  - go test didn't run because there's no Go code yet.

  Next unit: index_build, then retrieval. It builds the keyword (BM25) and
  meaning-based (BGE-small/FAISS) indexes for each piece size, merges both
  searches with RRF, and enforces the context cap. The first run downloads
  BGE-small, about 130 MB.

  Before phase 1 can finish: its done-check ("the right passages come back for
  the dev questions") needs eval/questions.jsonl, the 30 questions with gold
  answers. Do you want to write them, or should I draft them for you to check
  and change? The brief values questions you wrote yourself.

  What I didn't check: table header lines can show a blank spacer column as
  col4, which is harmless. I also haven't read through every table piece by
  hand. Nothing has been committed yet.

  1. Broad questions became specific ones.
     - "What experiments do the authors use?" can't be graded right or wrong, so
       it became "What average accuracy does the 2-stage H-Net reach versus the
       Transformer?" (55.5 vs 53.3).

       it became a question about the paper's specific sentence on why recurrent
       models can't be parallelised.
  2. Three answers come from tables and can't be guessed: AIAYN single-head BLEU
     (24.9 vs 25.8), Moshi's spoken QA accuracy with and without Inner
     Monologue (26.6 vs 9.2 on Web Questions), and the H-Net numbers above.
  3. Most refusals are now near-misses, not easy ones. Questions like "GPT-5.6"
     or "autonomous driving" are trivial to refuse because search finds nothing
     related. Near-miss questions find evidence that looks relevant, so they
     test whether the system refuses anyway. For example:
     - q17 asks for English-Romanian BLEU, and search returns the BLEU tables.
     - q18 asks for inference speed on a P100, and both "P100" and "inference"
       appear in the paper.

       appear only in the Moshi paper, so this tests whether the system wrongly
       credits Moshi's results to the Transformer paper.
     - q30 asks for Moshi's "dynamic chunking" settings, but dynamic chunking
       belongs to the H-Net paper.
  4. I replaced your idea 30 (autonomous driving) with q30 above, because
     driving is too easy to refuse.

✻ Crunched for 2m 57s · done Thursday 4:44 PM

❯ So tell me one thing these gold answer is what if the user ask similar        
  question then this automated answer comes or it is for testing of our system? 

● They're only for testing. The live system never sees them.

  When a user asks a question, even one worded exactly like q05, the answer is
  built fresh:

  1. Search the papers for the most relevant passages.
  2. Send those passages to the Groq model, which writes an answer with
     citations.
  3. The verifier checks every claim against the passages it cites.
  4. The user gets the verified answer, or a refusal if the papers don't support
     one.

  Nothing in that path reads eval/questions.jsonl. DESIGN §8.1 states it
  explicitly: the request may carry a question_id, but "the app must not use it
  to answer".

  The gold answers are an answer key. After a test run, we compare what the
  system answered against them and grade each reply as correct, wrong, correctly
  refused or wrongly refused. Those grades fill the answer_grade column in
  results.csv and the quality numbers in Tables 2b and 3.

  Why they must never be served: if the system answered from the answer key, the
  eval would only measure whether it can look up our own file. The grades would
  be meaningless, and a reviewer would rightly treat that as cheating.

  Two things that look similar but aren't:
  - The cache (built late, off in every experiment) stores answers the system
    itself generated and verified, never the gold answers.
  - The stand-in's replies replay answers the real Groq model gave earlier,
    recorded during real runs. They're used for load tests, which measure speed
    and failures, not answer quality.

  Eight questions is a small sample, so treat these as directions, not final
  numbers.

  What this shows:
  1. Reranking is the biggest single gain: from 50% to 87.5% of questions
     getting at least one gold passage.
  2. Four 256-token passages are too few. They fill only about 800 of the
     2,500-token cap, so questions that need 3–4 pieces of evidence lose some.
     Setting C gets more in only because its pieces are twice as long.
  3. The cross-paper question q14 fails in every setting. It needs evidence from
     both AIAYN and HNET, but all four passages come from HNET. This is one of
     the "misleads a naive retriever" examples the write-up needs.
  4. Unanswerable questions score as high as answerable ones. q24 (emotion
     recognition) has a top similarity of 0.81, and q16 (dollar cost) has a
     reranker score of 3.9. A score threshold alone won't refuse them. Phase 2's
     deterministic evidence check has to do that job, which the design already
     expects.

  Your decisions:
  1. Passages per question. Should settings A, B and D take more 256-token
     passages, for example 8, so that A/B/D and C use about the same tokens and
     Table 3 compares them fairly? I recommend 8, measured against the token
     cost. The alternative is to keep 4 as DESIGN says.
  2. Cross-paper questions. When a question names two papers, should search take
     the best passages from each named paper separately? I recommend yes: it's
     about 10 lines, and it fixes q14 by design rather than by tuning. The
     alternative is to leave it and report it as a known failure.

  I've kept tuning on the dev split only, so the test split stays untouched, as
  DESIGN §19.3 requires.

❯ My decisions:                                                                 
  1. Increase retrieval depth, but compare by token budget rather than a fixed  
  passage count.                                                                
  2. Yes, enforce per-paper retrieval coverage when a question explicitly names 
  multiple papers.                                                              
     Both changes are justified by your current results, but implement them as  
  explicit retrieval policies rather than silently changing the evaluation.     
     Decision 1: Passage count                                                  
     Decision: use a comparable token budget                                    
     Your current results show that 256-token chunks retrieve less evidence     
  partly because four passages provide only around 800 context tokens, while    
  the 512-token setting provides around 1,426.                                  
                                                                                
  I recommend:                                                                  
  Setting    Chunk size    Initial retrieval depth                              
  A    256    8 passages                                                        
  B    256    8 passages                                                        
  C    512    4 passages                                                        
  D    256 or 512    Adjust to equivalent budget                                
                                                                                
  Use approximately 1,400–1,600 context tokens per question as the target       
  budget for this comparison.                                                   
                                                                                
  Important distinction:                                                        
  - Retrieval depth determines how many candidates are considered.              
  - Context budget determines how much evidence reaches the LLM.                
  - These should be independently configurable.                                 
    Don't simply increase top_k and assume all retrieved passages should enter  
  the final context. Let the context builder enforce the token cap.             
                                                                                
  For Table 3, report the actual context tokens consumed, not just the number   
  of passages. This makes the comparison more defensible.                       
  Decision 2: Cross-paper retrieval                                             
  Decision: enforce per-paper coverage                                          
  When a question explicitly names two papers, retrieve evidence from both.     
                                                                                
  For example, q14 should not receive four HNET passages just because HNET has  
  higher similarity scores.                                                     
                                                                                
  I recommend this approach:                                                    
  1. Detect the paper IDs explicitly mentioned in the question.                 
  2. Retrieve candidates independently from each named paper.                   
  3. Reserve at least one passage from each paper.                              
  4. Merge the candidates.                                                      
  5. Apply reranking globally.                                                  
  6. Build the final context under the same token budget.                       
     For a two-paper comparison, an initial allocation of two passages per      
  paper is reasonable when the budget allows it.                                
                                                                                
  Do not apply this policy to every question. Ordinary questions should retain  
  global retrieval across the entire paper library. Only explicit multi-paper   
  questions should activate the constraint.                                     
  Additional observations                                                       
  Three things need attention before you move to phase 2:                       
                                                                                
  1. q14 is a retrieval-policy failure, not simply a reranker failure.          
                                                                                
  The reranker cannot select evidence that the candidate retrieval stage never  
  supplies. Your per-paper constraint addresses that upstream problem.          
                                                                                
  2. Don't introduce a similarity threshold to refuse unanswerable questions.   
                                                                                
  Your q24 and q16 results demonstrate why. A high similarity score does not    
  establish that the retrieved passage supports the requested claim. Phase 2    
  should verify whether the evidence actually supports the answer.              
                                                                                
  3. Keep the test split untouched.                                             
                                                                                
  Continue tuning on the dev split. Once retrieval settings and policies are    
  finalized, run the test split once and report the results separately.         

● Clear. I'll implement both as explicit, configurable policies:

    to the context builder) and a new context_budget (how many tokens may reach
    the model) become separate settings. The context builder enforces the
    smaller of the setting's budget and the current pressure cap.
  - Per-paper coverage: it switches on only when a question explicitly names two
    or more papers.

● Both policies are in place as configurable settings, and the dev results
  improved. All 114 tests pass. q14 now gets passages from both papers, but its
  gold passages still don't come back, for a different reason explained below.

  What changed:
  - Passage depth and token budget are separate. final_passages is how many
    ranked passages go to the context builder (8 for A/B/D, 4 for C).
    context_budget is 1,600 tokens for every setting. The builder applies
    whichever is tighter: the budget or the pressure level's cap. So Table 3
    compares settings at the same budget, and the done-check reports the tokens
    actually used.
  - Per-paper coverage (paper_mentions.py) switches on only when a question
    names two or more papers explicitly. Then candidates are retrieved within
    each named paper, reranked together, and 2 passages per paper are pulled to
    the front before the token cap applies. The cap can drop the second pair but
    never the first, so at least one passage per paper always survives. This is
    configurable as retrieval_policy.cross_paper_reserve_per_paper in
    config/app.yaml.
    - Which questions trigger it: only q14 and q15. A bare "Transformer" doesn't
      count as naming AIAYN, because the other papers use it for their own
      parts ("RQ-Transformer", "BPE Transformer"). q30 ("Moshi's dynamic
      chunking layer") stays single-paper, so that misleading question isn't
      helped.
  - No similarity threshold for refusal. Phase 2's evidence check decides
    refusals.

  Dev results at 1,600 tokens (8 answerable questions, so treat these as

● Phase 2's first units are built, but the sufficiency check needs a decision

  Done and tested (11 new tests, all passing):
  - relay/llm/prompts.py: the system prompt, the user message with passages, the
    redraft message, and the refusal and busy wording, all per §13. A test

  Written but not yet tested: relay/verify/evidence.py (level 2: numbers with
  units, key terms, the paper named) and relay/verify/sufficiency.py (§14.4).

  The problem: the sufficiency check asks whether the question's "key terms"
  appear together in the retrieved passages. §14.4 defines key terms as words
  that are rare in the corpus, or not in it at all. That picks up question
  phrasing instead of content:
  - "prevents" and "matter" (q01), "decide" and "go" (q05) and "segmented" (q14)
    are rare, so each causes a refusal.
  - "Mimi", "emotion" and "Inner Monologue" are common in their paper, so they
    don't count, and q24 (emotion recognition) gets through.

  The check runs before the model call. So every question it refuses saves about
  3.5K tokens of the daily budget, and every wrong refusal costs a correct
  answer. It isn't the last line of defence: the model can still reply
  NOT_IN_PAPERS, and the verifier still checks every sentence of the answer.
  Without part-of-speech information, a word-list check can't tell question
  phrasing from content. Adding "go" or "matter" to a stopword list would just
  tune it to these 15 dev questions.

  Decision needed: which rule should the sufficiency check use?
  1. Structural only (recommended). Refuse only when nothing was retrieved or a
     named paper is missing. Refusal then rests on the model and the verifier,
     which is where §2.2 puts correctness anyway. It's the only rule with no
     false refusals. The cost is spending tokens on unanswerable questions, and
     we'd measure how often the model refuses on its own once real calls run.
  2. "Technical terms always count, other words only if rare." This is the best
     trade-off of the word-list rules: 1–2 false refusals, and it catches 4 of 7
     unanswerable questions before any tokens are spent.
  3. Keep the rule as designed and report its false refusals.

  The same key-term definition is also used in verifier level 2 on answers,
  where a false rejection means refusing a correct answer. For that I'd use
  "known rare words plus unseen technical terms", so the model's ordinary
  paraphrasing never fails a sentence but invented model names or wrong numbers
  still do. Is that OK too?

  Not done yet: tests for evidence and sufficiency (they wait on your choice),
  and the draft → verify → refuse path run against a fake model. No Groq calls
  have been made.

✻ Baked for 3m 46s · done Thursday 8:34 PM

❯ Do not use the key-term rule as a pre-model refusal mechanism.                
                                                                                
  Your measurements show that the current lexical approach creates too many     
  false refusals. A system that refuses answerable questions before consulting  
  the model is violating the more important requirement: answering questions    
  when the papers contain sufficient evidence.                                  
  1. Pre-model sufficiency check                                                
     Use these structural conditions:                                           
  - At least one usable passage must be retrieved.                              
  - If the question explicitly names multiple papers, at least one passage from 
  each named paper must survive retrieval.                                      
  - The retrieved context must not be empty after applying the context budget.  
    If these conditions fail, refuse before calling Groq.                       
                                                                                
  Otherwise, allow the model to attempt an answer.                              
                                                                                
  Do not interpret missing rare words as proof that evidence is insufficient.   
  2. Verifier level 2                                                           
  Your proposed approach is acceptable, with one important modification.        
                                                                                
  Use known rare terms and unseen technical-looking terms as warning signals,   
  not automatic rejection conditions.                                           
                                                                                
  For example:                                                                  
  Generated claim    Treatment                                                  
  Correct paraphrase using ordinary vocabulary    Accept if supported by        
  evidence                                                                      
  Incorrect model or architecture name    Flag for evidence verification        
  Invented numerical result    Flag for evidence verification                   
  Technical term absent from the retrieved evidence    Investigate whether the  
  claim is supported                                                            
  Different wording expressing a supported concept    Do not reject solely      
  because the words differ                                                      
                                                                                
  The verifier should establish semantic support, not lexical overlap.          
                                                                                
  An invented technical term should not automatically fail a sentence if the    
  underlying claim is still supported. Conversely, a familiar term should not   
  make an unsupported claim acceptable.                                         
  3. Recommended verification flow                                              
                                                                                
  Question                                                                      
     |                                                                          
     v                                                                          
  Retrieve passages                                                             
     |                                                                          
     v                                                                          
  Structural sufficiency check                                                  
     |

     Add tests for:                                                             
  1. An answerable question with common terminology.                            
  2. An answerable question using a paraphrase absent from the paper.           
  3. An unanswerable question with highly similar retrieved passages.           
  4. A question explicitly naming two papers when one paper has no retrieved    
  passage.

  6. An answer containing an unsupported numerical result.

  terminology.                                                                  
     Also test the full refusal path against a fake model. Confirm that         
  structural failures do not call the model and that lexical mismatches do not  
  cause premature refusals.                                                     
  5. Record this design decision                                                
     Update DESIGN §14.4 and the change log:                                    
  - Pre-model sufficiency is structural, not lexical.                           
  - Lexical rarity is not evidence of answerability.                            
  - Level 2 uses terminology as a diagnostic signal, not a standalone rejection 
  rule.                                                                         
  - Semantic evidence support determines whether generated claims are           
  acceptable.                                                                   
    One final evaluation requirement: Measure unanswerable-question refusal     
  accuracy after real model calls. Report both refusal accuracy and             
  false-refusal rate on answerable questions. Also report token consumption,    
  since structural-only checking will send more unanswerable questions to the   
  model.                                                                        

● Clear. This changes the verifier's design: "semantic support decides" means
  level 2's term and number checks become warning flags, and the accept/reject
  decision needs a semantic check. Under the hard rules that must be local, not
  an LLM call, which is exactly DESIGN's level 3: a small NLI model that tests
  whether the cited passage entails the sentence. I'll build it now, because the
  required tests depend on it. First I'm checking a candidate NLI model on
  example pairs from the papers.

● Phase 2's code is written and all 163 tests pass. One thing blocks finishing
  it: the small NLI model is too strict to make the accept/reject decision. I'm

  Built so far, following your flow:
  - verify/sufficiency.py: structural checks only. It refuses before the model
    when no usable passage reaches the context, or when a question names several
    papers and one of them has no passage.
  - verify/citations.py (level 1): rejects a sentence with no citation, or one
    citing a chunk that doesn't exist or wasn't retrieved for this question.
  - verify/evidence.py (level 2): now only flags: numbers or units missing from
    the cited passage, technical-looking or rare terms missing from it, and a
    named paper that isn't cited. Ordinary words that differ from the paper's
    wording are never flagged.
  - verify/nli.py and verify/verifier.py: semantic support decides. Each
    sentence needs an NLI entailment of at least 0.5 from its cited passages, or
    at least 0.8 if level 2 flagged it. Both thresholds are placeholders in
    config/app.yaml, to be fitted on the verifier stress set.
  - pipeline.py: retrieve → structural check → draft → verify → one redraft →
    answer or refuse.
  - DESIGN §14.3–14.5 are rewritten with your four decisions, and the change log
    is updated.

  Tests: 163 passed, 0 failed. All seven cases you listed are covered, using a
  fake NLI model whose scores each test sets. The tests also confirm two things:
  structural failures never call the model (it records zero calls), and a word
  the papers never use ("segmented") doesn't cause a refusal before the model is
  asked. With the fake model, a wrong number is caught and fixed by the
  redraft, an invented answer is refused after the redraft, and NOT_IN_PAPERS
  becomes a refusal.

  What this shows:
  1. Entailment as a hard gate rejects correct answers with either model. The
     base model handles ordinary paraphrase well (0.991). It still can't accept
     the claim naming "Mimi", because the cited chunk says "We use Q = 8
     quantizers" and never names Mimi, so the claim is technically unproven from
     that passage alone. It also can't follow "d_k = d_model/h = 64" to
     "64-dimensional heads".
  2. Contradiction is a strong reject signal: both models give the wrong number
     above 0.95.
  3. The other unsupported claims come out neutral, not contradicted. Here level
     2's flags do the work: "512", "three weeks" and "RQ-Transformer" are all
     missing from the passage and would be flagged.

  That suggests a rule I haven't adopted yet, because it changes your "semantic
  support decides" decision in one respect:
  - Reject any sentence the NLI model contradicts.
  - A flagged sentence (missing number, technical term or attribution) must be
    entailed.
  - An unflagged sentence is accepted unless it's contradicted.

  On these 7 pairs it gets 6 of 7 right. The miss is the "Mimi" restatement,
  which stays flagged because "Mimi" isn't in the cited chunk. Its blind spot is
  a claim in ordinary words that adds an unsupported idea without a number or

❯ Yes. Build the verifier stress set before choosing the final NLI model or     
  acceptance rule. Do not commit the current placeholder thresholds yet.        
                                                                                
  The seven hand-made pairs establish that entailment-only verification is too  
  strict, but they are insufficient to establish that contradiction-or-flag is  
  reliable.                                                                     
                                                                                
  I would make the following changes to the proposed experiment.                
  1. Build a 40-pair stress set                                                 
  Use 20 supported and 20 unsupported claim/evidence pairs, drawn from the      
  actual three papers.                                                          
  Category    Supported    Unsupported                                          
  Exact factual restatements    3    2                                          
  Semantic paraphrases    4    2                                                
  Technical paraphrases    3    2                                               
  Implicit entity references    3    2                                          
  Numerical and unit claims    2    4                                           
  Model/architecture attribution    2    3                                      
  Experimental details and added claims    3    5                               
  Total    20    20                                                             
                                                                                
  Include cases such as:                                                        
  - A chunk says Q = 8 quantizers; the generated claim identifies Mimi.         
  - A chunk gives \(d_k = 64\); the generated claim says each attention head    
  has 64 dimensions.                                                            
  - A chunk describes recurrent processing; the answer paraphrases its effect   
  on parallelization.                                                           
  - A claim attributes an experiment to the wrong model.                        
  - A claim uses the correct metric but invents its numerical value.            
  - A claim combines a supported fact with an unsupported additional assertion. 
  The last category is particularly important. Your verifier must not accept an 
  entire sentence just because part of it is supported.                         
  2. Compare both verification policies                                         
  Run both models against both policies.                                        
  Policy    Acceptance condition                                                
  P1: Entailment-gated    Accept only if entailment exceeds the configured      
  threshold                                                                     
  P2: Contradiction-or-flag    Reject if contradicted; require entailment for   
  flagged claims; otherwise accept unless contradicted                          
                                                                                
  Measure:                                                                      
  - False acceptance rate: unsupported claims accepted.                         
  - False rejection rate: supported claims rejected.                            
  - Overall accuracy.                                                           
  - Per-category false acceptance and rejection.                                
  - Average verification latency per answer.                                    
  - P50 and P95 latency.                                                        
  Don't select a model based on overall accuracy alone. A verifier that accepts 
  invented facts is particularly problematic for this assignment.               
  3. Fix one important issue in the experiment                                  
  Evaluate claims against all passages cited for that claim, not just one       
  isolated passage.                                                             
                                                                                
  For example, if one passage describes eight quantizers and another identifies 
  the audio codec as Mimi, the combined evidence may support the claim.         
                                                                                
  Otherwise, you risk measuring missing context rather than NLI capability.     
                                                                                
  Keep the evidence boundaries explicit: only passages actually retrieved and   
  cited for that answer should be considered.                                   
  4. Separate calibration from evaluation                                       
  Use this process:                                                             
  1. Build the 40 pairs.                                                        
  2. Split them into 25 calibration pairs and 15 held-out pairs, balanced by    
  outcome.                                                                      
  3. Use calibration pairs to choose thresholds.                                
  4. Freeze the model, thresholds and decision policy.                          
  5. Evaluate once on the held-out pairs.                                       
  6. Report the limitations of the small dataset.                               
  Do not use your 15 question evaluation set to tune NLI thresholds.            
  5. My provisional preference                                                  
  Candidate to test: P2                                                         
  Contradiction-or-flag is more promising than strict entailment gating based   
  on your current observations. However, its main weakness is important:        
                                                                                
  An unsupported claim can receive a neutral NLI score and contain no obvious   
  lexical flag. P2 could accept it.                                             
                                                                                
  That is why your stress set must include unsupported claims expressed in      
  ordinary language, without unusual terminology, numbers or model names.       
                                                                                
  Also, keep the evidence verifier's lexical flags as diagnostic signals. They  
  should not independently establish factual correctness.                       
  Implementation instruction                                                    
  Build the stress set and evaluation harness first. Run the four combinations  
  (two models × two policies), save the raw scores and decisions, and produce a 
  comparison report.                                                            
                                                                                
  Do not make Groq calls yet. Do not change the retrieval evaluation dataset.   
  Do not lower thresholds simply to make the existing seven examples pass.      
                                                                                
  The decision should be based on the held-out results, especially the false    
  acceptance rate. A verifier that occasionally rejects a correct paraphrase is 
  undesirable; one that confidently accepts invented research findings is       
  worse.                                                                        

● Clear. Here's the plan:

  1. Write 40 claim/evidence pairs from real chunks.
  2. Write a harness that scores every pair once per model and stores the raw
     scores.

  What each failure means:
  - base + P2 accepts invented claims. It wrongly accepted u06 (the
    cosine-similarity rule reversed) and u17 (a true fact plus an invented
    "deduplicated against the benchmarks"). Both came out neutral, not
    contradicted, and level 2 flagged neither: exactly the blind spot you
    predicted. It also accepted u08, below.
  - base + P1 rejects correct claims. On calibration it rejected 8 of 12
    supported claims, including the "Mimi + 8 quantizers" claim even with both
    passages joined, and the "64-dimensional heads" paraphrase. If a sentence
    fails with probability 0.4–0.67, a typical 4-sentence answer almost never
    passes whole. So in practice it would refuse almost everything.
  - u08 defeats both policies. "Mimi uses distillation to make its tokens
    non-causal" reverses the paper's causal/non-causal relation. The base model
    gives it entailment 0.996.
  - The small model is worse on both counts. I'd drop it.

  Two level 2 flag defects show up on calibration pairs:
  1. "one for itself and one for the user" gets read as the number 1.
  2. Ordinary words that happen to be rare in the corpus ("lets",
     "parallelized", "generalize") get flagged.

  I haven't fixed them. Fixing them and re-scoring the same held-out pairs would
  amount to tuning on those pairs.

  About the sample size: each held-out unsupported pair is 14.3 points, so these
  are directions, not precise rates. The report is in
  eval/reports/verifier_stress.json with every raw score, and DESIGN §20.3 has
  the summary.

  Your options:
  1. base + P1, dropping failed sentences instead of refusing the whole answer.
     This is the safest against invented findings, but many correct sentences
     get dropped, so answers will be short or replaced by "The papers do not
     state…". Real-model runs would show the cost.
  2. base + P2, reporting the false-acceptance rate honestly as the known limit.
     Answers rarely get refused, but added claims in ordinary words get
     through.
  3. (My recommendation) Test one stronger NLI model before choosing. For
     example MoritzLaurer/DeBERTa-v3-base-mnli-fever-anli, which is trained on
     harder adversarial data. It needs a new set of held-out pairs, because
     these 15 have now been seen. I'd write 20 fresh pairs, fix the two flag
     defects on calibration data first, then evaluate once. The cost is a
     download of about 700 MB and a few hours of work. If it doesn't beat base +
     P1 on false acceptance with a usable false-rejection rate, fall back to
     option 1.

  Whichever you choose, the verifier adds about 2.2 s per answer at the median
  (about 3.2 s at p95, assuming four claims), all before the first token,
  because the answer is verified before it's sent.

     - Rarity no longer creates a flag. Only name-like terms are flagged now (a

     The full sentence stays in the list because "X because Y" can invent the
     link between two true facts. For example, u17 "…essential for stable
     training, and removing it also doubles the training time" is checked as the
     whole sentence, plus "The smoothing module is essential for stable
     training.", plus "Removing it also doubles the training time.".

  Must fix

  1. The claim splitter cuts lists and time phrases into fragments with no verb
     (relay/verify/claims.py:L15-18)
     - What this is: In "atomic" mode, a sentence is split at connector words,
       and every piece must be confirmed by the NLI model (the local model that
       judges whether a passage supports a claim).
     - Problem: The splitter also cuts:
       - lists: "The encoder uses self-attention, feed-forward layers, and
         residual connections around each sub-layer." gives the fragment
         "Residual connections around each sub-layer.";
       - "since" used about time: "…has existed since the 2017 paper was
         published." gives "The 2017 paper was published.".

       A fragment with no verb can't be "supported", so a correct sentence fails
       in atomic mode. None of the 40 new pairs is a list sentence, so the
       coming run won't show this, but the model's real answers often contain
       lists.
     - Fix: Don't split at ", and" when the text before it already has a comma
       (that makes it a list), and drop since from the connectors. That's two
       small edits in the regex and loop, plus one test with a list sentence.
     - If we skip it: Atomic mode looks safe in the stress test, then rejects
       correct list-style answers once it's in use.

  Should fix

  2. No test covers the list and "since" cases (tests/unit/test_claims.py)
     - What this is: These tests check how sentences get split.
     - Problem: They only cover connectors that do start a clause. No test fails
       if lists get split, which is exactly the bug in finding 1.
     - Fix: Add one test that a three-item list sentence stays whole.
     - If we skip it: The bug can come back silently.

  Nice to have

  3. The p95 time per answer is overstated
     (relay/eval/stress_verifier.py:L131-134)
     - What this is: The report estimates verification time per answer as 4 ×
       the time per sentence.
     - Problem: Four times the slowest 5% of single sentences is larger than the
       slowest 5% of four-sentence totals. So the "p95 per answer" figure is
       too high, while p50 is about right.
     - Fix: Report p95 per sentence only, and say the per-answer figure is "4 ×
       p50". Or sum 4 randomly chosen sentence times, repeated many times, and
       take the p95 of those sums.
     - If we skip it: The latency trade-off looks worse than it is when you
       choose between models.

  Groq docs report. Question 2 is only partly answered: the pages I read do not
  say where streaming usage appears.

  1. Reasoning controls for openai/gpt-oss-120b and openai/gpt-oss-20b
  - reasoning_effort: allowed values are low, medium, high. The API reference
  says "'medium' is the default value." Other values are rejected: "Values
  outside a model's supported set are rejected with a 400."
  - reasoning_format: not supported. The reasoning page says: "With
  `openai/gpt-oss-20b` and `openai/gpt-oss-120b`, the `reasoning_format`
  parameter is not supported."
  - include_reasoning: supported. Default is true. "false: Excludes reasoning
  from the response." Setting include_reasoning to false is how reasoning is
  hidden.
  - Mutually exclusive: yes. The API reference says include_reasoning "is
  mutually exclusive with `reasoning_format`." The reasoning page says the same.
  - By default, gpt-oss returns reasoning in message.reasoning.
  - Caveat: the reasoning page's general parameter table lists the
  reasoning_format default as raw. That conflicts with its gpt-oss section,
  which says the parameter is not supported for gpt-oss, so rely on the gpt-oss
  section.

  2. Token usage with stream: true
  - Not stated in any page read. The reasoning page's streaming example and the
  OpenAI-compatibility page do not mention usage.
  - The API reference's non-streaming example shows a top-level "usage" object
  with prompt_tokens, completion_tokens, total_tokens, plus queue_time,
  prompt_time, completion_time, total_time. Its x_groq object holds only "id".
  - No reasoning-token field is documented for chat completions.
  output_tokens_details.reasoning_tokens appears only on the Responses API
  object.
  - stream_options is described as "Options for streaming response. Only set
  this when you set `stream: true`." It lists no properties, so include_usage is
  not confirmed.
  - Correction: the API-reference summary I received said the chat section was
  missing. It was in the readable text. Only the streaming usage details are
  missing.

  3. Rate-limit headers
  - Per-day requests (RPD): x-ratelimit-limit-requests,
  x-ratelimit-remaining-requests, x-ratelimit-reset-requests. Each "Always
  refers to Requests Per Day (RPD)."
  - Per-minute tokens (TPM): x-ratelimit-limit-tokens,
  x-ratelimit-remaining-tokens, x-ratelimit-reset-tokens. Each "Always refers to
  Tokens Per Minute (TPM)."
  - Reset format: examples are "2m59.56s" (requests) and "7.66s" (tokens),
  labeled "illustrative." Other formats: not stated.
  - retry-after: "In seconds" (example value 2). Set only on a 429: "retry-after
  is only set if you hit the rate limit and status code 429 is returned."
  - ITPM/OTPM headers are not listed. Some organizations have separate ITPM/OTPM
  limits, visible on the Limits page.

  4. 429 response
  - Status: 429 Too Many Requests.
  - retry-after: present on a 429, in seconds.
  - JSON error body shape (error.message, error.type, error.code): not stated.
  - How the body says which limit was hit: not stated. The docs say only that
  "You can hit any limit type depending on which threshold you reach first."

  5. max_tokens vs max_completion_tokens
  - max_completion_tokens is preferred. max_tokens is "Deprecated in favor of
  `max_completion_tokens`."
  - The reasoning page gives a default of 1024 for max_completion_tokens and
  says complex proofs may need higher limits. It does not single out gpt-oss.

  Extra, from the rate-limit page (organization-wide limits for both gpt-oss
  models): 30 RPM, 1K RPD, 8K TPM, 200K TPD. "Cached tokens do not count towards
  your rate limits."

  Pages read (final URLs):
  - https://console.groq.com/docs/reasoning.md
  - https://console.groq.com/docs/rate-limits.md
  - https://console.groq.com/docs/api-reference (partly readable; the truncated
  remainder was summarized)
  - https://console.groq.com/docs/openai.md (no usage or reasoning details)

  Time per sentence is about 445 ms at the median and 580 ms at p95 for whole
  sentences, and about 516 ms / 1,618 ms with atomic splitting. Each held-out
  pair is worth 12–14 points, so read these as directions.

  What it shows:
  - P1 (entailment-gated) beats P2 for both models. P2 lets through
    ordinary-language claims that are neutral and unflagged.
  - Atomic splitting didn't help. It caught no unsupported claim that
    whole-sentence checking missed (the invented clause in u17 was already
    rejected), and it rejected correct compound sentences (s09, s19).
  - ANLI + P1 whole is the best balance:
    - its one false acceptance is u08 ("all four DNA models were H-Nets", when
      two of the four weren't);
    - its false rejections include s02, a word-for-word sentence from the paper,
      scored at 0.563.
  - base + P1 never accepted an invented claim, but it rejects about 60% of
    correct sentences, so most real answers would end up refused.

  Built for the real request:
  - relay/llm/client.py: the streaming Groq client.
    - It follows Groq's docs: max_completion_tokens, reasoning_effort: low, and
      include_reasoning: false to hide the reasoning.
    - It records first byte, first answer token and last token, plus the
      rate-limit headers and token usage.
    - Every call is appended to results/raw/real/, never with the key.
    - Without LLM_PROVIDER=groq it points at the stand-in, so nothing can spend
      quota by accident.
  - relay/governor/: per-model limits on requests and tokens per minute and per
    day. Every call reserves first, then settles to actual usage and resyncs

● The first real end-to-end requests ran, using 7 of the 8 approved calls. The
  pipeline itself works: every call went to the right model, token accounting is
  exact, no key reached any log, and there were no 429s. But the provisional
  verifier refused both answerable questions even though the model's answers
  were correct.

  Pre-call checks: both model IDs were right, the answer limit was 900
  completion tokens, all 207 tests passed (including key exclusion), and
  reservations were checked.

  Calls 1–2, model checks (188 tokens):
  - Both models exist and answered from the right model.
  - Token-accounting gap, found and fixed: gpt-oss adds a fixed 67-token
    preamble to every request (Groq reported 78 prompt tokens where I counted
    11, on both models). I added it to config/app.yaml as measured. Afterwards
    my estimate matched Groq's count within ±1 token, and no reservation was
    exceeded. This was the only stop condition that came close; it was a fixed,
    explained offset that the correction then confirmed, so I continued.
  - Facts for Table 1:
    - Reasoning tokens are reported (14–73 per call).
    - Usage arrives in the top-level usage field.
    - The daily request limit refills continuously, one request every 86.4 s
      (reset showed 1m26.4s after one of 1,000).
    - Per-minute tokens look separate for each model.

  Calls 3–7, questions (dev split, setting B):

  Why the two correct answers were refused:
  1. Answers written in LaTeX (q05). All three sentences in the first draft were
     correct. NLI accepted one (0.94) and rejected two (0.84, 0.60). The
     redraft repeated the accepted claim, and it then scored only 0.63. Level 2
     also flagged the LaTeX command \tfrac12 as a "technical term".
  2. Table rows (q11). "Single-head development BLEU of 24.9 [AIAYN:T3:r02]" is
     exactly right, but NLI scored it 0.03 and 0.09 against the row text (A): h 
     = 1; …; BLEU / (dev) = 24.9. The model can't read our row format. The model
     correctly said the base model's BLEU "is not stated", because that row
     wasn't retrieved (the q11 retrieval miss we already knew about).

  On q16 the model refused on its own, so the verifier wasn't needed.

  One quota detail I can't fully explain: Groq's per-minute reset time sometimes
  implies a few hundred more tokens than the usage it reports (first q05 call:
  about 2,331 vs 1,930). The governor follows the header, so it stays on the
  safe side. Limit probing should explain it.

  I didn't tune anything on these three questions. Everything is recorded in
  DESIGN §20.3, and the raw records are in results/raw/real/ and
  results/raw/e2e/. The files are dated 2026-11-12 because file names use UTC.

  What this means: two of the verifier's failure modes, LaTeX and table rows,
  are systematic, not chance. They would push the false-refusal rate on maths-
  and table-heavy questions far above the 25% the stress test measured, because
  the stress pairs contained no LaTeX and only one table row. Both can be fixed
  without touching any threshold:
  - Tell the model to write in plain text instead of LaTeX. That's a prompt
    change, which bumps prompt_version.
  - Rewrite table rows into sentences before NLI scoring ("With h = 1, the
    development BLEU is 24.9").

  Each fix needs a fresh stress round that includes LaTeX and table-row pairs
  before it's adopted. Do you want me to do that next, or would you rather
  decide first?

  The full evaluation hasn't run, nothing is committed, and about 10K of today's
  roughly 200K tokens are used.

  Diagnostic    What to establish

  Retrieved evidence    Did the cited passages support those claims?            
  Sentence decomposition    How many sentences were evaluated?                  
  NLI entailment    What score did each sentence receive?                       
  NLI contradiction    Was a correct claim classified as contradictory?         
  Level 2 flags    Which terms, numbers or entities triggered stricter          
  verification?                                                                 
  Threshold    Which threshold was applied to each sentence?                    
  Final decision    Which exact condition caused refusal?                       
                                                                                
  3. Do not tune against these two questions.                                   
                                                                                
  These are real end-to-end observations, not a new verifier evaluation set.    
  Record them as operational findings. If you change the verifier, document the 
  change and evaluate it on fresh evidence pairs.                               
  What I need before making the next verifier decision                          
  Share the remaining real-call results, especially:                            
  - q05 complete output and verifier trace.                                     
  - q11 complete output and verifier trace.                                     
  - q16 result, including whether it correctly refused.                         
  - The reason each answerable response was refused.                            
    The distinction matters: if the NLI score is low, this is a                 
  calibration/generalization problem. If the evidence flags are wrong, it is a  
  verifier implementation problem. If the citations point to insufficient       
  passages, it may be a retrieval or answer-generation problem.

● Both answerable refusals come down mainly to NLI scores that are low on
  correct claims, with retrieval misses as secondary causes. The level 2 flags
  didn't change either outcome. Every rejection was the same condition: best
  entailment below 0.9. I didn't spend the 8th call.

  q05: "How does H-Net's routing module decide where chunk boundaries go?" 
  Refused, wrongly.
  - Retrieved: 7 HNET passages, including the gold one, HNET:2.2.1:c023. Every
    sentence cited it.
  - Evidence the model saw: "The routing module implements this intuition
    through cosine similarity between adjacent encoder outputs … q_t = W_q x̂_t,
    k_t = W_k x̂_t, p_t = ½(1 − cos) ∈ [0,1], b_t = 𝟙{p_t ≥ 0.5}, where p_1 = 1.0
    … ensuring the sequence begins with a boundary." It also says boundaries
    emerge at "contextual or semantic shift" and that consecutive vectors there
    "should exhibit lower similarity".

  Why it was refused:
  1. Calibration/generalization (main cause). The same correct claim scored
     0.935 in draft 1 and 0.631 in draft 2. The only difference was LaTeX
     spelling (\bigl( versus \!\left(). The stress pairs contained no LaTeX.
  2. Each sentence is judged without its neighbours. Draft 2 S2 begins "It then
     forms…", and the model can't know what "It" refers to.
  3. Retrieval (partly). S3 is stated almost word for word in HNET:2.2.1:c024
     ("low cosine similarity and consequently high boundary probability"), which
     wasn't retrieved; that's the known q05 retrieval miss. So S3 was cited to
     a passage that supports it only indirectly (neutral 0.363).
  4. One flag defect, harmless here. The LaTeX command tfrac12 was flagged as a
     "technical term". The flagged threshold equals the normal one, so it didn't
     change anything.

  Why it was refused:
  1. Calibration/generalization. A correct claim, read against a table row,
     comes out leaning towards contradiction (0.54). The likeliest reason is
     that the same passage lists sibling rows with other BLEU values (25.5,
     25.8), plus the row format itself. The stress set had only one table-row
     pair.
  2. A verifier implementation gap, and it matters: the "papers do not state"
     sentence is exempt from every check, so a false "not stated" passes
     untouched. Here it was false only because retrieval missed the base row, so
     the model couldn't see it. Had the first sentence passed, the user would
     have been told the paper doesn't give the base BLEU, which is wrong.
  3. Retrieval. The base row is the known q11 retrieval miss.

    the verifier wasn't involved.
  - Cost: 1 call, 1,836 tokens. That's the token cost of the structural-only
    check, which rightly lets this question reach the model.

  Classification against your three cases:

  Cause: Low NLI score on correct claims (calibration/generalization)
  q05: main cause (LaTeX variance, lost "It" context)
  q11: main cause (table-row premise, contradiction-leaning)

  q11: none

  q05: partly (S3's best evidence, c024, not retrieved)
  q11: base row not retrieved, which led to a false "not stated"
  ────────────────────────────────────────
  Cause: Other implementation gap
  q05: —
  q11: exempt "not stated" sentences are never checked

❯ The real-call diagnostics identify implementation and evidence-handling       
  defects. Make the following changes before any more Groq calls.               
                                                                                
  P0 — Refusal explanations:                                                    
  - Remove the unconditional verifier exemption for "The papers do not          
  state..." sentences.                                                          
  - Verify explanatory refusal sentences like ordinary factual claims.          
  - Keep NOT_IN_PAPERS as a control signal, not an unchecked factual statement. 
  - If absence cannot be established, use wording limited to insufficient       
  retrieved evidence.                                                           
                                                                                
  P1 — NLI context:                                                             
  - Improve sentence-level verification by including the preceding sentence or  
  a short context window when resolving references such as "it" and "they".     
  - Keep each factual claim identifiable and independently verifiable.          
  - Add tests showing that context improves reference resolution without        
  allowing unsupported additions.                                               
                                                                                
  P2 — Table evidence:                                                          
  - Represent table rows as explicit structured evidence containing paper,      
  table, configuration, metric, split and value.                                
  - Ensure sibling rows cannot be mistaken for contradictory values for the     
  same configuration.                                                           
  - Improve retrieval of the AIAYN base configuration row.                      
  - Add tests for multiple configurations and numerical comparisons.            
                                                                                
  P3 — Evidence flags:                                                          
  - Normalize LaTeX notation before technical-term extraction.                  
  - Do not flag LaTeX macros such as tfrac12 as technical entities.             
                                                                                
  Keep ANLI + P1 at threshold 0.9 provisionally. Do not tune against q05/q11.

       94 +class PremiseNLI(FakeNLI):                                    
       95 +    """Entailment from (substring the premise must contain, hy
          +pothesis) rules; anything else is unsupported."""             
       96 +                                                              
       97 +    def __init__(self, rules: list[tuple[str, str, float]]):  
       98 +        super().__init__({})                                  
       99 +        self.rules, self.seen = rules, []                     
      100 +                                                              
      101 +    def predict(self, pairs):                                 
      102 +        import math                                           
      103 +        out = []                                              
      104 +        for premise, hyp in pairs:                            
      105 +            self.seen.append((premise, hyp))                  
      106 +            e = max([p for need, h, p in self.rules if need in
          + premise and h == hyp], default=0.02)                         
      107 +            rest = (1 - e) / 2                                
      108 +            out.append([math.log(rest), math.log(e), math.log(
          +rest)])                                                       
      109 +        return out                                            
      110 +                                                              
      111 +

● All four fixes are in, and the full suite passes (229 tests). No Groq calls
  were made; the real-call log still holds exactly 7, so the 8th approved call
  is unspent. The verifier is still ANLI + P1 at 0.9, and nothing was tuned on
  q05 or q11.

  P0, refusal explanations. The blanket exemption is gone.
  - The prompt (now p2) asks for "The retrieved passages do not state <missing 
    part>.", with no citation and no number.
  - Level 1 checks every such sentence: it must not cite and must not contain a
    value, because a value is itself a claim.
  - Any claim that "the papers / the paper / the authors do not state …" is
    rejected, since the model only saw the retrieved passages. That's the q11
    case.
  - An answer made only of absence sentences counts as a refusal.
  - NOT_IN_PAPERS stays a control signal. The refusal reply now reads: "I
    couldn't find this in the passages I retrieved from the three papers, so I
    won't guess. I searched: …", where before it claimed the papers don't state
    it.
  - Limit: whether the retrieved passages really lack the missing part can't be
    proven by entailment. Absence sentences are checked for scope and content,
    not for truth. This is recorded in DESIGN.

  P1, NLI context. A claim that opens with a reference word ("It", "They",
  "This", "These", …) is also scored with the previous sentence placed before
  each passage, but only if that sentence was accepted. The best score decides,
  so context can resolve "it" but can't add support the evidence lacks. The
  context used is recorded for each sentence.

  P2, table evidence.
  - Table chunks now carry structured rows: a configuration, plus column,
    metric, split and value for each cell. For example, "BLEU / (dev)" becomes
    metric BLEU, split dev.
  - Row lines read "Configuration base: … BLEU / (dev) = 25.8", and every
    existing gold quote still matches.
  - The verifier scores a table claim against each row alone ("Configuration
    (A): h is 1; BLEU (dev split) is 24.9."), so a sibling row is never next to
    the claimed value. It also scores against all rows as separate labelled 
    lines, so comparisons between rows can still be supported.
  - Retrieval: AIAYN Table 3's base row now ranks 2nd–3rd for base-configuration
    queries at both piece sizes, using keyword ranking.
  - The corpus was rebuilt as c2, along with both indexes.

  P3, evidence flags. Claims and passages are stripped of LaTeX before numbers
  and terms are extracted: delimiters, \commands (including shorthand like
  \tfrac12), escapes and braces. So tfrac12 is no longer a "technical term",
  while numbers written inside LaTeX are still checked.

  Regression tests added:

    among them); absence with a citation or a value rejected; an absence-only
    answer is a refusal; a partial answer with an unscoped sentence fails;
    refusal wording never claims the papers lack it
  ────────────────────────────────────────
  Issue: P1
  Tests: "It …" is resolved from an accepted previous sentence; an unsupported
    addition after "It" is still rejected; no context from a rejected sentence;
    no context without a reference word
  ────────────────────────────────────────

  Item 5, context from a rejected sentence. The mechanism held: p3's rejected
  first sentence passed no context on. But the following sentence, "It keeps
  continuous gradients…", was accepted on its own (0.996). The NLI model
  resolved "It" to the passage's subject (the Straight-Through Estimator), not
  to what the answer meant (the smoothing module). The whole answer still
  failed, because one rejected sentence fails it. Still, a pronoun sentence can
  be judged against a different referent than the one the answer means.

  Replays (observations, not tuned on):
  - q05: scores unchanged (0.935, 0.844, 0.601; 0.631, 0.611). The LaTeX fix
    changed only the flags; the NLI model still reads raw LaTeX. Draft 2's "It
    then forms…" got no context, because the sentence before it was rejected.
  - q11: the single-head BLEU claim scored 0.015 and 0.311 even against its own 
    row alone, so per-row premises didn't help. Its old "The papers do not
    state…" sentence is now rejected as unscoped, as intended.
  - q16: still refused correctly via NOT_IN_PAPERS (1 call), now with the reply
    worded about the retrieved passages.

  What this establishes: the local NLI model can't judge LaTeX formulas,
  comparisons across rows, or some pronoun sentences, at any threshold that
  keeps invented claims out. That's a model limitation, not a calibration knob.
  Fixing it would mean more verifier work: feeding NLI de-LaTeXed text, or
  adding a rule-based check of table values. You asked to avoid architecture
  expansion and move on, so here's how I'd proceed:

  1. Freeze verifier v2 at ANLI + P1, t = 0.9, as the production verifier.
     - It never accepted an unsupported held-out claim, which matches priority
       1: never send a wrong answer.
     - Its false-refusal rate on maths, table and comparison claims gets
       reported honestly in the write-up, which already has to say what each
       choice costs.
  2. (Optional, small) One prompt line asking the model to answer in plain text,
     not LaTeX (prompt p3). It costs nothing to build, and the real evaluation
     runs would show whether it helps. I'd only add it if you want it.
  3. Move to your priority list: the Go stand-in, the Go load generator, the
     five load scenarios, results.csv, the tables and the report.

  Shall I freeze the verifier, with or without the plain-text prompt line, and
  start on the stand-in?

  The NLI model is a big latency cost. At 1.3–3.1 s per answer it's a large
  share of the user-visible time, which will show up in the load tests. Nothing
  is committed, and the 8th call is preserved.

      148 +def tiers(df: pd.DataFrame) -> str:                           
      149 +    """What the users actually got. "Succeeded" in Table 2b co
          +unts refusals too; this separates them."""                    
      150 +    rows = []                                                 
      151 +    for name in LOAD_SCENARIOS + ["retrieval_A", "retrieval_B"
          +, "retrieval_C"]:                                             
      152 +        d = df[df["scenario"] == name]                        
      153 +        if d.empty:                                           
      154 +            continue                                          
      155 +        tier = d["answer_tier"].fillna("")                    
      156 +        rows.append([name, len(d), int((tier == "normal").sum(
          +)), int((tier == "refused").sum()),                           
      157 +                     int((tier == "unavailable").sum()), int((
          +d["status"] == "timeout").sum())])                            
      158 +    return table(["Scenario", "Requests", "Verified answer", "
          +Refusal", "Busy / unavailable", "Timed out or gave up"], rows)
      159 +

      161 +def verification(df: pd.DataFrame) -> str:                    
      162 +    """NLI verification time where NLI actually ran (> 50 ms).
          + Under 50 ms means no sentence reached NLI: the model         
      163 +    said NOT_IN_PAPERS, or level 1 rejected every sentence (e.
          +g. a fixture citing a chunk this setting did not              
      164 +    retrieve)."""                                             
      165 +    rows = []                                                 
      166 +    for name in LOAD_SCENARIOS + ["retrieval_A", "retrieval_B"
          +, "retrieval_C"]:                                             
      167 +        d = df[df["scenario"] == name]                        
      168 +        v = pd.to_numeric(d["verification_ms"], errors="coerce
          +").dropna()                                                   
      169 +        ran = v[v > 50]                                       
      170 +        if len(v):                                            
      171 +            rows.append([name, len(v), len(ran), duo(ran) if l
          +en(ran) else "-"])                                            
      172 +    return table(["Scenario", "Requests that reached verificat
          +ion", "NLI ran", "Verification p50 / p95 (ms) when NLI ran"], 
      173 +                 rows)

       1 +# The Relay — Akash Bisht
